title: From Experimentation to Enterprise AI Using Cisco AI POD on FlashStack
summary: Cisco AI POD with FlashStack for Secure Enterprise AI Factories solution, provides secure, scalable infrastructure for production AI inference, model serving, and enterprise AI applications.
body_markdown:
### Summary


The Cisco AI POD with FlashStack for Secure Enterprise AI Factories solution, jointly developed by Cisco and Everpure, provides secure, scalable infrastructure for production AI inference, model serving, and enterprise AI applications.


As organizations expand customer support agents, enterprise search, coding assistants, and other AI applications, more users compete for compute and storage capacity. Model updates can require old and new versions to run together. A server failure creates an urgent need to restore model instances while the remaining infrastructure continues serving requests. Enterprise teams must plan for these conditions alongside everyday demand.


The “Cisco AI POD with FlashStack® for Secure Enterprise AI Factories Design Guide,” developed jointly by Cisco and Everpure, addresses the infrastructure decisions behind those production demands. This Cisco Validated Design (CVD) defines a pre-validated, full-stack solution for deploying production inference in the data center with Cisco UCS compute, NVIDIA accelerated compute, NVIDIA AI Enterpirse software, Cisco Nexus networking, Everpure storage, and Red Hat OpenShift and OpenShift AI. It extends the Cisco AI POD for enterprise training and fine-tuning architecture with the compute, software, networking, management, and security capabilities required for inference—bringing the major solution elements together as an integrated path from infrastructure design to model serving and operations.


The design guide explains the architecture and design choices; the forthcoming deployment guide will document exact validated configurations, procedures, and test results.


[Read the “Cisco AI POD with FlashStack for Secure Enterprise AI Factories Design Guide](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/unified_computing/ucs/UCS_CVDs/flashstack_aipod_secure_enterprise_ai_factories_design_guide.html) .”


## More than a reference architecture


The solution is designed to be more than a list of compatible products. It brings compute, GPU acceleration, network fabrics, shared storage, Kubernetes, model-serving runtimes, management, observability, and security together under a common operating model.


That integration matters when teams need to move a service into production or change it without disrupting existing users. Compute capacity, storage access, network policy, model serving, and monitoring must work together. The guide gives architects and operations teams a shared design for those dependencies, reducing the integration decisions they would otherwise have to resolve independently.


The modular design also creates a practical adoption path. Organizations can start with a right-sized solution for their initial application portfolio, then incrementally add additional compute, fabric, storage, and serving capacity as demand grows. The architecture and management model remain consistent as the solution scales, avoiding a new integration exercise for every stage of the AI journey.


## Inference is an application platform problem


Production inference starts with applications, not with a single model. A typical application may combine a reasoning model with embedding, reranking, routing, vision, speech, guardrail, or other task-specific models. Different applications may also have different latency, throughput, concurrency, availability, data, and security requirements.


The infrastructure must therefore support both everyday demand and the changes that keep a business service running:


- Models may need to run concurrently, with replicas for availability and multiple versions for canary or A/B deployments.
- Long-context and reasoning workloads increase key-value cache requirements, while concurrent requests multiply the demand.
- Some models fit on one GPU, while others require multiple GPUs or multiple nodes.
- Agentic applications can generate several model, retrieval, and tool calls for a single user request.
- Shared infrastructure must provide predictable service and both performance and security isolation across teams and applications.


Planning for this combined demand helps teams assess whether another application or model version can be introduced while maintaining existing service levels. The guide translates that demand into compute, GPU, network, storage, Kubernetes, model-serving, and security choices.


## The solution: A full-stack path to enterprise inference


Meeting those requirements takes coordination all the way up the stack. The Cisco AI POD with FlashStack for Secure Enterprise AI Factories brings the following components together so that model serving, data access, infrastructure operations, and security can be planned as one complete service:


- Cisco UCS C845A M8 rack servers and Cisco UCS X-Series with X580p PCIe nodes as inference platform options
- Supported NVIDIA and AMD GPUs for different memory, compute, partitioning, and interconnect requirements
- Cisco Nexus 9000 Series switches for dedicated frontend and backend fabrics
- Everpure™ FlashBlade//S500 for shared file and object services, with[Portworx Enterprise](https://portworx.com/products/portworx-enterprise/) providing Kubernetes-native data services
- [Pure Key-Value Accelerator (KVA)](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/pure-kva-1-solution/) for a persistent, distributed KV cache that integrates with vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo, storing attention state on[FlashBlade](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/unstructured-data-storage.html) ® for reuse across requests and nodes to reduce repeated prefill work and support long-context, concurrent, and disaggregated inference
- Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA combines the integrated AI platform capabilities of Red


Hat AI Enterprise with NVIDIA AI Enterprise software to simplify the development and deployment of AI workloads on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure.


- Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform as the Kubernetes foundation and Red Hat OpenShift AI as the MLOps and model-serving platform
- KServe with vLLM, llm-d with vLLM, NVIDIA NIM™,, and NVIDIA Dynamo as model-serving options for different inference patterns NVIDIA NIM™,
- Cisco Intersight, Cisco Nexus Dashboard, and Cisco Cloud Control for infrastructure management and cross-domain operational context
- Security capabilities spanning Cisco Live Protect, Cisco Hypershield, Isovalent Cilium, and Cisco AI Defense


For NVIDIA deployments, the guide positions Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA as the recommended software path, combining Red Hat AI Enterprise and NVIDIA AI Enterprise in a jointly supported, co-engineered offering. This reinforces the solution approach: Customers receive an integrated platform and support model rather than assembling every software entitlement and runtime independently.


*Figure 1: The integrated technology stack defined by the Cisco AI POD for Enterprise Inferencing Design Guide.*


## Separating the fabrics to protect inference performance


The frontend fabric carries requests from the application to the inference servers and sends generated answers back. The backend fabric connects the GPUs doing the inference and carries communication among GPUs working together on the same model request.


These traffic patterns have different performance requirements. Frontend traffic is shaped by application demand and can surge unpredictably. A burst of customer requests can compete and disrupt the GPU-to-GPU coordination that produces each answer. Separate fabrics let the frontend scale and adapt to changing user demand while the backend is tuned for the GPUs’ steady, latency-sensitive communication. The separation is most useful when inference spans multiple servers or needs strong performance isolation.


This separation removes one source of contention for distributed model execution and allows the fabrics to be sized and expanded independently as the application portfolio grows. Frontend capacity must still accommodate application requests and storage bursts together.


For multi-node inference, the backend fabric uses a dedicated, non-blocking, lossless RoCEv2 design. The guide describes the roles of Priority Flow Control, Explicit Congestion Notification, congestion control, load balancing, and NVIDIA GPUDirect™ RDMA. Detailed queue, threshold, and deployment settings are reserved for the companion deployment guide, preserving a clear boundary between architectural guidance and prescriptive implementation details.


*Figure 2: Separate, dedicated frontend and backend networks.*


## Supporting multiple serving patterns


As inference demand grows, a service may need to scale in more than one way. The guide describes the following serving patterns:


- Single-GPU serving for models that fit within one GPU or GPU partition
- Multi-GPU serving within a node for models that exceed single-GPU capacity
- Multi-node tensor or pipeline parallelism for larger dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models
- Expert parallelism for MoE models, often combined with tensor or pipeline parallelism
- Disaggregated serving, which separates prefill from decode so each phase can be sized and scaled independently
- Replicas and horizontal scaling to increase throughput and availability without changing the parallelism configuration of every model instance


**The guidance is intentionally practical:** Start with the smallest GPU configuration that meets the model’s memory and performance requirements, then add replicas when throughput or availability requires it. Introduce multi-GPU, multi-node, or disaggregated serving when the model size, performance objective, or workload balance justifies the additional complexity—not by default.


## Storage and data management are part of the solution


Starting or restarting model instances, including adding replicas on additional servers, requires access to model data. Storage design affects how quickly that capacity becomes ready and how services recover. Model weights, model registry artifacts, application data, caches, and persistent volumes each have different performance, sharing, and persistence requirements. The updated design makes the storage architecture explicit by combining Everpure FlashBlade//S500 for shared file and object services with Portworx Enterprise for Kubernetes-native data services.


[Portworx](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/kubernetes-data-management.html) ® is integrated on the GPU worker nodes and uses local NVMe for its managed data services, while applications consume FlashBlade directly through NFS and S3. This distinction is important: Local NVMe that is not managed by Portworx is a reconstructable cache or staging tier, while Portworx-managed data receives its own protection and replication mechanisms.


Recovery requires protection for both the model artifacts used to rebuild a service and the persistent application data that cannot simply be recreated. Purity//FB SafeMode protects model registry buckets and critical file shares; FlashBlade replication supports recovery at a paired site where available; Portworx snapshots and CloudSnaps protect persistent volumes; and PX-Backup writes application-consistent backups to SafeMode-protected S3 repositories. This gives the platform a recovery model that spans storage, Kubernetes, and application data rather than relying on a single protection mechanism.


Finally, the design guide distinguishes the validated CVD reference from broader platform capability. The CVD validates a single FlashBlade//S500 chassis configuration with eXternal Fabric Modules (XFM), such as the XFM-8400R2, to interconnect chassis into a single namespace. This modular XFM architecture enables customers to scale storage bandwidth and capacity seamlessly across multiple chassis without requiring a complete redesign or disrupting operations. Scaling beyond this baseline configuration involves separate sizing with Everpure and confirmation against the current Portworx support matrix.


The solution uses a tiered approach:


- GPU memory for active model weights, runtime working memory, and active key-value cache data
- Host memory and local NVMe for runtime-supported caching, staging, and offload
- FlashBlade file services for hot shared data and model access over NFSv3 with RDMA where supported
- FlashBlade S3-compatible object services for versioned model artifacts and model registry references
- Portworx Enterprise for Kubernetes-native persistent volumes, snapshots, data protection, and data mobility


The guide now makes data placement a first-class design decision. Hot model weights and shared model caches use FlashBlade file services; model registry artifacts use versioned Purity//FB S3; per-pod and shared Kubernetes volumes use Portworx RWO and RWX services; and local NVMe supports model staging, pre-warming, caching, or runtime-supported key-value cache spill. The RoCEv2 backend fabric remains dedicated to GPU-to-GPU traffic rather than storage traffic.


## Security across the inference pipeline


As AI adoption grows, teams must control who can reach model endpoints, what enterprise data applications can access, and which tools agents can invoke. Production inference introduces risks that are specific to AI applications, including prompt injection, sensitive data leakage, unauthorized access to model endpoints, and unsafe agent or tool activity. The design therefore considers security at multiple layers rather than treating it as a separate perimeter function.


The guide describes complementary security controls across the stack, from infrastructure and Kubernetes to the AI application layer. Live Protect provides Cisco-validated Vulnerability Shields for disclosed vulnerabilities in Cisco network infrastructure without requiring device reloads or service interruption while software fixes are deployed; Cisco Hypershield provides distributed segmentation and policy enforcement across network and workloads, including Cisco Nexus Smart Switches and Kubernetes; Isovalent Cilium provides Kubernetes networking, visibility, and policy enforcement; and Cisco AI Defense protects the inferencing path by providing visibility and validation for AI applications, models, and agents, together with runtime protection for AI application and agent interactions against threats such as prompt injection, data leakage, and unsafe agent behavior.


The design also recognizes an important operational reality: Security capabilities must be introduced with clear scope and validation boundaries. The guide documents the architectural role of these controls, while the companion deployment guide will identify the specific capabilities and configurations included in CVD validation.


## A path from right-sized deployment to predictable scale


This architecture is modular by design, allowing organizations to scale predictably as demand grows. An organization can start with a single node or a few GPUs, then add compute, fabric, and storage capacity incrementally without redesigning the overall architecture. The frontend and backend fabrics, storage architecture, and management model remain consistent as the deployment expands.


The guide includes a sample bill of materials for a 32-GPU deployment using four Cisco UCS C845A M8 nodes. The Cisco Silicon One backend fabric supports up to 32 such nodes, or 256 GPUs, with one leaf pair. A second leaf pair extends the design to 64 nodes and 512 GPUs. These figures describe fabric connection capacity, not workload requirements or deployment size. The deployment must be sized separately. This sizing depends on the workload and model mix, parallelism strategy, replica count, storage requirements, and performance objectives.


This approach lets organizations align investment with demand. They can add nodes when models need more memory or compute, add replicas when request volume or availability requirements increase, expand storage as model versions and checkpoints accumulate, and scale prefill and decode pools independently when the workload benefits from disaggregation. The result is a predictable path from a small inference deployment to a larger FlashStack AI POD while preserving the same architectural foundation.


## From architecture to deployment


The design guide establishes the architectural decisions and scaling model. The forthcoming deployment guide will document the procedures and test coverage for implementing a selected reference deployment. Exact validated configurations, including storage capacity, throughput, failure testing, and performance acceptance criteria, remain tied to that documented scope.


Lifecycle automation supports repeatable deployment and operations through Cisco Nexus Dashboard fabric templates, Cisco Intersight profiles and policies, and OpenShift Operators for GPU, RDMA, storage, and platform services. Ansible automation is also planned as a follow-on to the deployment guide.


For enterprise teams, the practical starting point is to identify which applications and models must be served together, what service levels they need, and what capacity must remain available during updates and failures. The design guide provides a framework for translating those requirements into compute, network, storage, serving, and security decisions.


The FlashStack AI POD approach gives those teams a shared infrastructure blueprint for building, operating, and expanding production inference services.
